title: Coarctation of the aorta and interrupted aortic arch

paragraphs.text: 8 8 Coarctation of the Aorta and Interrupted Aortic Arch
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: In 1760, the Prussian anatomist Johann Friedreich Meckel characterized coarctation of the aorta as an “extraordinary dilatation of the heart which came from the fact that the aortic conduit was too narrow.”1 Saul Jarcho’s historical papers underscored the accuracy of early accounts of this congenital malformation.1–5
paragraphs.heading: HISTORICAL NOTES

paragraphs.text: Coarctation of the aorta is typically located near the aortic attachment of the ligamentum arteriosum or patent ductus arteriosus (Figs. 8.1A and 8.2). An obtuse indentation in the posterolateral wall of the aorta corresponds to the location of an internal ridge or shelf that eccentrically narrows the aortic lumen, hence the term coarctatus (Latin, contracted or tightened). The ridge that forms the coarctation consists of smooth muscle, fibrous tissue, and elastic tissue similar in composition to a muscular arterial ductus (see Chapter 17).6 Intimal proliferation distal to the ridge narrows the lumen.6 The junction between the ductus and the elastic aorta is clearly defined, with the extension of ductal tissue into the aortic wall not exceeding 30% of the aortic circumference. In preductal coarctation, however, ductal tissue forms a circumferential sling that extends around the aorta.7 In juxtaductal coarctation, ductal tissue is not a significant part of the aortic wall.7 The coarctation ridge is thought to represent the original wall of the distal left sixth aortic arch (see Chapter 17). The neural crest is believed to play a role in the pathogenesis of some types of coarctation.7
paragraphs.heading: COARCTATION OF THE AORTA Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: The common form of aortic coarctation is represented by a localized constriction containing the ridge or shelf as just described.6 Less commonly, a relatively long segment of constriction extends beyond the left subclavian artery. Rarely, congenital coarctation is in the mid-thoracic aorta.8 Tubular hypoplasia refers to a uniform narrowing within the aortic arch.6 Localized coarctation and tubular hypoplasia sometimes coexist.
paragraphs.heading: COARCTATION OF THE AORTA Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: The mechanisms that account for the typical location of coarctation take into account a number of variables: (1) the quantitative morphology and growth of the aortic arch in the normal fetus,9–11 (2) the site of the aortic orifice of the ductus arteriosus, (3) the presence of ductal tissue in the coarctation, 6 (4) constriction of ductal tissue immediately after birth, and (5) coarctation in the presence of a widely patent ductus in the fetus12,13 and after birth.6 Current consensus favors an interplay between aortic growth and blood flow.9–11 High-resolution echocardiographic imaging in the normal fetus has disclosed progressive tapering of the diameter of the aortic arch at all gestational ages with the smallest diameter at the isthmus.9 Tapering is believed to reflect the relative proportion of fetal cardiac output traversing each aortic segment. The smallest proportion traverses the isthmus, which maintains its smaller dimension relative to the remainder of the aortic arch well into postnatal life, especially in premature infants.9 Neonatal coarctation is characterized by hypoplasia of the transverse aorta in the presence of a relatively large pulmonary trunk, a combination that is believed to reflect an in utero decrease in aortic arch flow together with an increase in flow through the main pulmonary artery and ductus.11
paragraphs.heading: COARCTATION OF THE AORTA Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: The coarctation ridge is located either immediately proximal to the aortic insertion of the ductus, or opposite the aortic insertion (juxtaductal), or immediately distal to the aortic insertion.6,14,15 Infants with a juxtaductal coarctation show no signs of aortic obstruction as long as the ductus is widely patent, assuring unobstructed pulmonary trunk/ductus/descending aortic continuity. When the ductus closes, the coarctation becomes apparent immediately and dramatically, and the femoral pulses disappear. The left subclavian artery is dilated because coarctation is usually located immediately distal to its origin (see Figs. 8.1A and 8.3A). However, coarctation may lie at or proximal to the left subclavian orifice, compromising its lumen (see Fig. 8.1B and see Fig. 8.27, later). Exceptionally, the right subclavian artery arises distal to the coarctation (see Fig. 8.1C) or the coarctation is in a right aortic arch.16
paragraphs.heading: COARCTATION OF THE AORTA Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: Coarctation of the abdominal aorta can be part of a non-congenital systemic vascular disorder such as Takayasu arteritis or von Recklinghausen’s disease, but it can also be congenital and is therefore appropriate for inclusion here.17–20 Abdominal coarctation is rare, accounting for 0.5% to 2% of all varieties of aortic coarctation,18 and can be suprarenal, infrarenal, or inter-renal.18 Systemic hypertension is believed to be due to the involvement of the renal artery.20 A congenital etiology is based on the combination of a localized hourglass deformity with an intraluminal membrane, occurrence at a young age, absence of a systemic vascular disorder, and slow progression with the development of extensive collaterals.20
paragraphs.heading: COARCTATION OF THE AORTA Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: Pseudocoarctation refers to a rare anomaly characterized by buckling or kinking of the aorta in the vicinity of the ligamentum arteriosum, resulting in elongation, tortuosity, and dilatation of the distal aortic arch and the proximal descending aorta (Fig. 8.3).21–25 Occasionally, pseudocoarctation involves the abdominal aorta.26 Pseudo signifies the absence of a gradient at the site of the localized external deformity, absence of collaterals, and absence of systemic hypertension, although refractory hypertension has been reported.27 Occasionally, there is a transformation from pseudocoarctation to true coarctation.28 The femoral pulses are sometimes reduced because of the damping effect of sharp angulation of the aortic arch (Fig. 8.4).22 Thin-walled saccular aneurysms may form in the distal segment,21 spontaneous rupture and dissection have been reported in the proximal descending thoracic aorta29 and in the ascending aorta,30 and bicuspid aortic valve may coexist.31 The strongest association is with a functionally normal, stenotic, or incompetent bicuspid aortic valve (Fig. 8.5B and see Chapter 7)32,33 characterized by a fusion of the right and left coronary cusps.33,34 When aortic dissection occurs with coarctation that co-exists with a bicuspid aortic valve, adverse outcomes are more pronounced, suggesting that the bicuspid aortic valve may represent an advanced manifestation of a more diffuse arteriopathy.35
paragraphs.heading: COARCTATION OF THE AORTA Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: Coarctation of the aorta is usually and simplistically regarded as isolated obstruction of the aortic isthmus,36 but in fact is a widespread disorder in which isthmic obstruction is only one of a cluster of abnormalities that include the proximal and distal paracoarctation aorta, the ascending and transverse aorta, the coronary arteries, conduit arteries (radial, brachial, carotid), the retinal vascular bed, dissecting aneurysm, cerebral aneurysms, vascular rings, and systemic hypertension. paragraphs.text: Arterial collaterals are important vascular sequelae of coarcta - tion, and their development depends on subclavian artery patency (Figs. 8.7 and 8.5A). When coarctation obstructs the orifice of the left subclavian artery, ipsilateral collaterals fail to develop (see Fig. 8.27, later). A subclavian steal may result from retrograde flow down the ipsilateral vertebral artery.53 Systemic-to-pulmonary collaterals normally present after birth gradually disappear.54
paragraphs.heading: COARCTATION OF THE AORTA Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: Retinal arterioles are the site of a distinctive vascular pattern.52,55 In 1948, at the annual meeting of the Swedish Ophthalmological Society, Professor K.O. Granstrom stated, “As in other cases of hypertension, these patients are sent as a matter of routine for examination to the eye department. As soon as I had seen a few such cases, it became evident that the retinal picture in coarctation of the aorta is often somewhat characteristic, the principal feature being pronounced tortuosity of the arteries.”5 6 The U-shaped tortuous retinal arterioles (Fig. 8.8) may be ac - companied by serpentine pulsations synchronous with the arte - rial pulse.55 Granstrom correctly concluded that the distinctive retinal abnormality in coarctation was benign and that hypertensive retinopathy was conspicuous by its absence.56
paragraphs.heading: COARCTATION OF THE AORTA Anatomic Considerations

paragraphs.text: Coarctation of the aorta can contribute to a vascular ring that consists of a double aortic arch or a right aortic arch, a left ligamentum arteriosum, and an aberrant subclavian artery.57–59 An anomalous retroesophageal right subclavian artery occasionally accompanies coarctation of the aorta (see Fig. 8.1C) but does not cause tracheoesophageal compression.

paragraphs.text: The pathogenesis of systemic hypertension in coarctation of the aorta has been the subject of three theories. The mechanical theory focuses on resistance at the site of obstruction. This theory in itself cannot be sustained but is central to the neural theory that involves the sensitivity of carotid sinus baroreceptors and the distensibility characteristics of the precoarctation aorta.60 The proximal aortic segment of coarctation has an increase in collagen and a decrease in smooth muscle60 that are responsible for an increase in stiffness and a decrease in distensibility.61 The poorly compliant precoarctation aorta is responsible for the elevation of systolic blood pressure at rest, the disproportionate rise during isotonic exercise,62,63 and the resetting of carotid sinus baroreceptors to operate at higher pressures.60,62 The renal theory of pathogenesis takes into account a unique feature of coarctation hypertension, namely, that the elevated blood pressure is confined to the upper extremities. Accordingly, the renal arteries are exposed to the neurohumoral effects of hypertension but not the hydraulic effects. The coarctation gradient increases during isotonic exercise, which is accompanied by a disproportionate increase in systolic pressure,64 an exaggeration of the inherent disproportionate systolic hypertension related to the rigidity of the precoarctation aortic wall. The response of the mean blood pressure to exercise is approximately the same as in controls.65 Experimental hypertension has been produced by aortic constriction that assigns the renal arteries to the distal low-pressure zone.66 When the constriction is below the renal arteries, blood pressure remains normal.66,67 Toxemia of pregnancy is not a feature of coarctation hypertension.

paragraphs.text: Eye grounds do not exhibit hypertensive retinopathy but instead exhibit distinctive serpentine retinal arterioles (see Fig. 8.8).52,55
paragraphs.heading: Physiologic Consequences

paragraphs.text: The increase in left ventricular mass induced by the afterload of coarctation is characterized by myocyte replication rather than myocyte hypertrophy,68 which is believed to account for reduced end-systolic wall stress and enhanced left ventricular ejection performance.69
paragraphs.heading: Physiologic Consequences

paragraphs.text: The male/female ratio of coarctation is 1.4:1 to 3:1.70 Familial recurrence has occurred in siblings, in monozygotic twins, in parent and child,71–76 and as an autosomal dominant in four generations.77 True coarctation and pseudocoarctation have been reported in siblings.78 Turner syndrome (see Physical Appearance) cannot be transmitted because of sterility, but seven women in three generations of one family had Turner syndrome attributed to loss of the short arm of one X chromosome that permitted transmission from phenotypically normal female carriers with a balanced X-1 translocation.79 There is a peak seasonal incidence of coarctation from September through November and from January through March.80 The reported rarity of coarctation in African Americans is open to question.81,82
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Coarctation of the aorta usually produces significant symptoms in early infancy,70,83,84 and after age 20 to 30 years.85 Neonates with severe coarctation become acutely symptomatic when the ductus closes. Survival has been reported at age 74 years and 76 years.87 Isolated atresia of the aortic arch was surgically repaired at age 65 years.88 The longest recorded survival was Reynaud’s account (1828) of a 92-year-old man with coarctation.3 The anatomic illustrations in this report are noteworthy. However, examples of exceptional longevity should not obscure the inherent risk of coarctation that results in death at an average age of 33 years.
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Mild coarctation is not always benign, and severe coarctation is not always symptomatic. A case in point, albeit rare, is a 20-year-old woman with severe coarctation, borderline hypertension, and no symptoms.89 Except for symptomatic infants, patients tend to be clinically well when the diagnosis is first made. Initial suspicion requires little more than attention to upper and lower extremity arterial pulses and blood pressure (see The

Nevertheless, delayed recognition is not uncommon,90,91 and diagnoses have been made by chance in the fifth decade.92 Minor symptoms include epistaxis and leg fatigue. When coarctation compromises the orifice of the left subclavian artery in left-handed patients, muscular fatigue involves the left arm. Leg fatigue occurs in about half of patients, but claudication is reserved for abdominal coarctation. Patients are sometimes subjectively aware of amplified arterial pulsations in the neck, especially after effort or excitement. Dysphagia occurs when a retroesophageal right subclavian artery originates distal to the coarctation and passes behind the esophagus,93 (see Fig. 8.1C) or when coarctation is a component of a vascular ring.
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Major symptoms are features of four eventualities: (1) congestive heart failure, (2) rupture or dissection of the aorta, (3) infective endarteritis or endocarditis, and (4) cerebral hemorrhage.84,85,94–96 Hypertension is chiefly responsible for morbidity and mortality

paragraphs.text: The rupture originates in either a paracoarctation aneurysm,48,49,95 or above a coexisting bicuspid aortic valve because of an inherent medial abnormality of the ascending aorta (see Chapter 7).49,95,98 Rupture of a postcoarctation aneurysm may be accompanied by bleeding into the esophagus that is announced by hematemesis and melena. In XO Turner syndrome (see Physical Appearance), rupture or dissection of an ascending aortic aneurysm occurs because of an inherent medial abnormality49 whether or not there is coexisting coarctation or a bicuspid aortic valve (Fig. 8.11).104–106 Aneurysms of intercostal arteries are almost always occult and relatively benign.50 Pseudocoarctation has been regarded as a disorder that incurs little or no risk, but the malformation is not necessarily benign and is not necessarily pseudo (see earlier). Pseudocoarctation has been reported with Turner syndrome.107 Cerebral arterial aneurysms are discussed under cerebrovascular accidents (see later).
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Infective endarteritis or endocarditis is a major complication of coarctation of the aorta, although the more susceptible site is a coexisting bicuspid aortic valve (see Chapter 7).84,98 Saccular septic aneurysms are occasional sequelae of infective endarteritis.95,108
paragraphs.heading: The History

paragraphs.text: Cerebrovascular accidents are the fourth major eventuality in coarctation of the aorta.84,94,109 Intracranial aneurysms have a prevalence of about 10% in patients with coarctation, where they are more common than in the general population.35,110 Hypertension is not a necessary precondition because cerebral complications can occur in normotensive patients long after a successful repair. An aneurysm of the circle of Willis, first described in 1927,111 is the chief offender (see Fig. 8.6) and sets the stage for rupture and cerebral hemorrhage.112 Less common, but not less important, are aneurysms in other cerebral arteries.94 Infective endocarditis on a bicuspid aortic valve can give rise to septic cerebral aneurysms that rupture. Rarely and oddly, an unruptured intracranial aneurysm triggers musical hallucinations.113

paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance

paragraphs.text: XO Turner syndrome, with its distinctive physical appearance (Fig. 8.12), arouses suspicion of coarctation of the aorta.120,121 Chromosomal patterns 45 XO and X-mosaicism are coupled with additional cardiac expressions.122–125 Aortic rupture or dissection in Turner syndrome was mentioned earlier (see Fig. 8.11).104,105,126 The typical XO Turner phenotypic female (Fig. 8.13) is of short stature with webbing of the neck, absent or scanty auxiliary and pubic hair (ovarian dysgenesis), broad chest with widely spaced hypoplastic or inverted nipples, low anterior and posterior hairlines, small chin, prominent ears because of large auricles, cubitus valgus, short fourth metacarpals and metatarsals, distal palmar triaxial radii, narrow hyperconvex nails, and pigmented cutaneous nevi.121 Infants with Turner syndrome exhibit lymphedema of the neck with loose skin, puffiness of the dorsum of the hands and feet, and low hairlines.121,127 Congenital heart disease is much more frequent in Turner syndrome with webbing of the neck than in Turner syndrome without webbing,122,127 and coarctation of the aorta is eight times as frequent when Turner syndrome is accompanied by webbing of the neck.127 Noonan syndrome (Turner phenotype with normal genotype) (see Fig. 8.12) is only occasionally accompanied by coarctation of the aorta128 and rarely by ascending aortic aneurysm.96,121,129 Systemic hypertension in Turner syndrome occurs without coarctation. paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance

paragraphs.text: Abnormal differences in upper and lower extremity arterial pulses and blood pressure are hallmarks of coarctation of the aorta. If proper attention were given to these pulses, few or no diagnoses would be missed.91,132 Two methods have been advocated for comparing upper and lower extremity arterial pulsations. One method compares femoral and radial pulses; the other method compares femoral and brachial pulses. Normally, radial and femoral pulses are sensed as synchronous so that any femoral delay is considered abnormal. Positioning the patient’s wrist next to the groin is believed to facilitate comparison. In infants and newborns, the brachial artery is more readily palpated than the tiny radial artery, which is surrounded by subcutaneous fat pads (Fig. 8.14B). Comparative palpation of brachial and femoral pulses can be achieved by placing a thumb on each (see Fig. 8.14A).132 The slight delay in perceived arrival time of the normal femoral pulse (15 ms in adults, less in infants and children) is easily sensed as a norm against which even slight deviations can be judged. When palpating the femoral pulse in an infant, the patient must be allowed to relax its legs voluntarily because forceful restraint can decrease or abolish a normal femoral pulse.

paragraphs.text: What is perceived as an abnormal delay of the femoral pulse in coarctation is not a delay in arrival time but instead a slow rate of rise to a delayed peak (Fig. 8.15). paragraphs.text: Bicuspid aortic regurgitation reinforces the femoral pulse, which can be misjudged unless properly compared with the brachial pulse (Fig. 8.16A).133 Bicuspid aortic stenosis may not dampen the brachial arterial pulse because coarctation amplifies the ascending aortic and brachial arterial systolic pressures (see Fig. 8.16B).133 Conversely, if aortic stenosis dampens the ascending aortic systolic pressure, evidence of coarctation is obscured (see Fig. 8.16C).133
paragraphs.heading: The Arterial Pulse

paragraphs.text: The right and left brachial arteries should be compared by palpation and by cuff blood pressure (see Fig. 8.14B). A decreased or absent left brachial arterial pulse indicates that the coarctation has compromised the lumen of the left subclavian artery (see Fig. 8.1B) or is proximal to its origin (see earlier). When comparing the two brachial pulses, account must be taken of normal systolic pressure differences of 10 to 15 mm Hg lower in the left arm.132 Diminution or absence of the right brachial pulse implies that the right subclavian artery originates distal to the coarctation (see Fig. 8.1C). The absence of both brachial arterial pulses signifies that coarctation is compromising the lumen of the left subclavian artery while the right subclavian artery arises distal to the coarctation.134 At birth, femoral arterial pulses are temporarily palpable if the coarctation is juxtaductal, if the ductus is distal to the coarctation, or if the aortic end of the ductus is patent.6 The abdominal aorta is readily palpable proximal to abdominal coarctation but is not palpable when coarctation is in the aortic isthmus. Pseudocoarctation leaves the arterial pulses normal because there is no aortic obstruction, although angulation at the level of the ligamentum arteriosum occasionally dampens the femoral pulses (see Fig. 8.4).22

paragraphs.text: Upper extremity blood pressure in infants and adults is usually recorded in the supine position, but a comfortable sitting position in a parent’s lap is acceptable for relaxation of infants and young children. Lower extremity blood pressure is best determined from the popliteal artery with the patient prone.132 A thigh cuff is applied while the popliteal artery is palpated and must be inflated slowly to avoid discomfort. The cuff is inflated to a level just above the brachial arterial systolic pressure until the popliteal pulse vanishes. Systolic and diastolic pressures are then estimated by auscultation of popliteal Korotkoff sounds. Diagnostic differences in arm and leg blood pressures are based on systolic levels when only systolic Korotkoff sounds are heard. However, the diastolic pressures are important in confirming accuracy because they are not significantly different in the upper and lower extremities (see Fig. 8.15). When intraarterial systolic, diastolic, and mean brachial and femoral pressures are compared in normal persons, there is no significant difference, although the femoral auscultatory systolic pressure is about 10 mm Hg higher than the direct femoral arterial pressure.140 Differences between the arm and leg systolic pressures in coarctation are exaggerated by exercise, which causes an increase in brachial arterial pressure, with no change or a reduction in femoral arterial pressure.141 Coarctation of the aorta is accompanied by a progressive, age-related increase in blood pressure, especially systolic, so the pulse pressure widens.62,74

paragraphs.text: Coarctation of the aorta is associated with systolic, diastolic, and continuous murmurs (Fig. 8.17). An ejection sound is an auscultatory sign of a coexisting bicuspid aortic valve (see Figs. 8.17 and 8.18). Systolic murmurs originate from three sources (see Fig. 8.17): (1) arterial collaterals, (2) the coarctation itself, and (3) the brachiocephalic arteries. That murmurs can originate in collateral arteries is based on observations that localized superficial collateral murmurs are abolished by compression and that murmurs have been recorded from the surfaces of surgically exposed collateral arteries.145 A murmur cannot be generated across coarctation when the obstruction is complete (see Fig. 8.7B), but murmurs are prominent because arterial collaterals are well developed (see Fig. 8.7A and C).145 The widespread anatomic distribution of the collateral arterial circulation accounts for the widespread thoracic distribution of accompanying murmurs.146 Collateral murmurs are crescendo-decrescendo and are delayed in onset and termination because they originate at a distance from the heart (see Figs. 8.17, 8.19, and 8.20).145 Widely distributed thoracic murmurs constitute presumptive evidence of collateral circulation, but in young children, collaterals may be well developed without generating murmurs, and in occasional adults with abundant collaterals, murmurs are inconspicuous.

paragraphs.text: Notching of the ribs is a classic radiologic sign of coarctation caused by collateral flow through dilated, tortuous, pulsatile posterior intercostal arteries (see Figs. 8.7, 8.9, and 8.26). Notches vary from rib to rib and from patient to patient and may be single, multiple, shallow, deep, broad, or narrow.42,149 Notching originates in posterior intercostal arteries that run in intercostal grooves (see Fig. 8.9), so the anterior ribs are spared because anterior intercostal arteries do not run in intercostal grooves.149,150 Rarely, the superior margin of a rib is notched because of contact with an overhanging intercostal artery.151 Rib notching seldom appears before age six years, although exceptional examples have been described as early as two years of age.42,150,152

The development of arterial collaterals depends on the patency of the ipsilateral subclavian artery, so when the left subclavian lumen is compromised, ipsilateral collaterals fail to develop, and unilateral rib notching is confined to the right hemithorax (Fig. 8.27).149,150 Anomalous origin of the right subclavian artery distal to the coarctation (see Fig. 8.1C) results in failure of collateral development in the right hemithorax, so unilateral notching is confined to the left hemithorax.93,150 Lateral x-rays show retrosternal notching or scalloping caused by dilated tortuous internal mammary arteries (see Fig. 8.7A and B).42,152 When coarctation is in the abdominal aorta, notching, if present at all, is confined to the lower ribs.153

The suprasternal notch window with color flow imaging identifies the coarctation by a zone of localized accelerated flow and by providing the target through which the continuous wave Doppler beam can be aligned to determine the gradient (see Figs. 8.29, 8.30, and 8.31).155,156 Peak systolic velocity reflects the maximum systolic gradient, and persistent high velocity diastolic forward flow indicates severity (see Figs. 8.29B and 8.31B).155–157 The Doppler pattern across the coarctation is affected by reduced proximal aortic compliance.158 Color flow identifies the level at which laminar flow becomes turbulent (see Fig. 8.29C). paragraphs.text: Coarctation of the aorta will not be overlooked if attention is given to upper and lower extremity arterial pulses and blood pressure during routine physical examination. The diagnosis is evident when systemic hypertension is accompanied by reduced femoral pulses. Aortic coarctation is a widespread disorder in which isthmic obstruction is only one of an array of abnormalities that include abnormalities of the proximal and distal paracoarctation aorta, abnormalities of the ascending and transverse aorta, the conduit arteries (radial, brachial, carotid), the retinal vascular bed, in addition to systemic hypertension, dissecting aneurysm, cerebral aneurysms, and vascular rings. Minor symptoms include headache, epistaxis, and leg fatigue. Major complications are congestive heart failure, especially in infants, rupture or dissection of the paracoarctation aorta, infective endarteritis, and rupture of an aneurysm of the circle of Willis. The physical appearance of XO Turner syndrome increases the probability of coarctation. Pulse pressure proximal to the coarctation increases with age, resulting in conspicuous carotid and suprasternal notch pulsations. Collateral arterial pulsations should be sought beneath the skin, especially around the scapulae. Tortuous U-shaped retinal arterioles are distinctive. A left ventricular impulse occupies the apex. A right ventricular impulse is reserved for symptomatic infants with heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, and a right-to-left shunt across a patent foramen ovale. Auscultatory

paragraphs.text: signs include widespread thoracic systolic murmurs through arterial collaterals and a posterior systolic or continuous murmur over the coarctation site. Systolic murmurs are especially prominent in the suprasternal notch and along the left sternal border over internal mammary collaterals. Auscultatory signs in infants are limited to the posterior interscapular murmur over the coarctation. Electrocardiographic criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy reflect increased afterload. Right ventricular hypertrophy characterizes the electrocardiogram of symptomatic infants. Notching of the third to eighth posterior ribs is a radiologic feature of major diagnostic importance but is seldom present before age six years. Dilatation of both the left subclavian artery and the proximal descending aorta are useful radiologic signs in children too young to have rib notching. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiograms with Doppler interrogation and color flow imaging identify the coarctation and determine its severity.
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: The thoracic aorta lends itself to the segmental analysis of its ascending portion, arch, isthmus, and descending portion. Atresia or interruption of the aortic arch is the ultimate expression of obstructive thoracic aortic anomalies that begin with isthmic coarctation. The embryogenesis of these anomalies is similar, if not identical.
paragraphs.heading: INTERRUPTION OF THE AORTIC ARCH

paragraphs.text: Interruption of the aortic arch was first described in the 18th century by Raphael Steidele of the University of Vienna.159 Steidele’s complex is occasionally applied as an eponym to this rare malformation,160,161 which is characterized by a complete anatomic discontinuity or by an atretic fibrous strand between the aortic arch and the descending aorta (Fig. 8.32).162–165 The classification of complete interruption by Celoria and Patton163 refers to one of three sites,160,161,165,166 two of which were described in 1927 by Maude Abbott.167 Interruption between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries (type B) (see Figs. 8.32 and 8.33) is more common than interruption distal to the left subclavian artery (type A). The least common site is between the innominate artery and the left carotid artery (type C) (Fig. 8.34).163,168,169 Subtypes are based on the anomalous origin of the right subclavian artery.134,168,170 Rarely, interruption is in a right aortic arch.171
paragraphs.heading: INTERRUPTION OF THE AORTIC ARCH

paragraphs.text: Interruption of the aortic arch seldom occurs as an isolated anomaly.172–175 Patent ductus arteriosus and ventricular septal defect are coexisting malformations upon which tenuous neonatal survival depends. The clinical picture in infants is largely determined by the patency of the ductus arteriosus, which provides nonrestrictive flow from the pulmonary trunk into the descending aorta (see Fig. 8.32).160,164,165 In the majority of patients with interrupted aortic arch, the ductus is histologically mature with prominent intimal cushions that prefigure constriction. In a minority of patients, an immature ductus is devoid of intimal cushions and has marked elastification that sets the stage for persistent patency. A ventricular septal defect almost invariably coexists when the interruption is between the left carotid and left subclavian arteries (type B), and it coexists in about 50% of interruptions distal to the left subclavian artery (type A).43,160,164–166,168,173 A posterior malaligned ventricular septal defect is the rule when the interrupted arch is between the left carotid and left subclavian arteries (type B).162,166,176 Defects in the perimembranous and muscular septum are uncommon.43 Posterior deviation of the infundibular septum encroaches on the left ventricular outflow tract and causes subaortic obstruction.43,166 When the ventricular septum is intact, a physiologically equivalent aortopulmonary window is almost always present,177 and the interrupted arch is distal to the left subclavian artery (type A).177

paragraphs.text: Complete interruption of the aortic arch is estimated to occur in 19 per million live births, according to the New England Regional Infant Cardiac Program.184 Males and females are equally represented.160,161,165 Recurrence has been reported in siblings,185–188 and a 2.5% recurrence rate of congenital heart disease has been reported in siblings of patients with type B interruption.189

paragraphs.heading: Physical Appearance

paragraphs.text: Femoral arterial pulses are maintained because of continuity between the pulmonary trunk, ductus, and descending aorta (see Fig. 8.32).165,173,191 A reduction in femoral pulses signifies ductal constriction, which initially may be intermittent.173 When the left subclavian artery originates from the descending aorta (type B), ductal constriction reduces the left brachial pulse in addition to the femoral pulse. Anomalous origin of the right subclavian artery places the right brachial pulse in the distal low-pressure zone.170 On the rare occasion of interruption of the aortic arch or arch atresia without patent ductus or ventricular septal defect, palpation of the systemic arterial pulses is analogous to palpation in coarctation of the aorta.134,172–174,180,181 When an interruption occurs proximal to both subclavian arteries (anomalous origin of the right subclavian), the carotid pulses are bounding, but the brachial and femoral pulses are diminished or absent.134,174,181 If
paragraphs.heading: The Arterial Pulse

paragraphs.text: either or both subclavian arteries originate proximal to the interruption, the arms will be hypertensive, the carotid pulses will be bounding, and the femoral pulses will be weak or absent.172,181
paragraphs.heading: The Arterial Pulse

paragraphs.text: An isolated right ventricular impulse is palpated in infants with interruption of the aortic arch because of obligatory pulmonary hypertension and is associated with a nonrestrictive patent ductus arteriosus and ventricular septal defect. A left ventricular impulse is absent despite the left-to-right shunt at the ventricular level because blood entering the pulmonary trunk is diverted through the ductus into the descending aorta rather than through the pulmonary circulation into the left side of the heart (see Fig. 8.32). Interruption of the aortic arch without patent ductus or ventricular septal defect results in a left ventricular impulse analogous to coarctation of the aorta.181
paragraphs.heading: Precordial Movement and Palpation

paragraphs.text: Murmurs are negligible or absent.165 The ductus is silent because the shunt is entirely right-to-left through a single nonrestrictive arterial conduit formed by continuity of the pulmonary trunk, ductus, and descending aorta. Murmurs originating through the ventricular septal defect are early systolic, decrescendo, and grade 3/6 or less.191,201 A continuous murmur has been attributed to collateral circulation connecting the ascending and descending aortas.191 Diastolic murmurs due to pulmonary hypertensive pulmonary regurgitation165 are introduced by a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound. Interruption of the aortic arch without a ductus or ventricular septal defect presents with auscultatory signs similar to those of imperforate coarctation, with widespread collateral murmurs that include the head, especially behind the ears.172,181,202
paragraphs.heading: Auscultation

paragraphs.text: Peaked right atrial P waves and right ventricular hypertrophy are electrocardiographic features in the neonate with interruption of the aortic arch, ventricular septal defect, and patent ductus arteriosus (Fig. 8.35).201 Biventricular hypertrophy is in response to left ventricular volume overload and persistent right ventricular pressure overload (Fig. 8.36).165 Interruption without patent ductus or ventricular septal defect results in right ventricular hypertrophy in infants,134 but left ventricular hypertrophy in older patients.
paragraphs.heading: The Electrocardiogram

paragraphs.text: The cardiac silhouette enlarges, and pulmonary venous congestion develops rapidly when the closure of the ductus arteriosus suddenly causes an increase in pulmonary blood flow and volume overload of the left ventricle. The aortic knuckle is absent because the ascending aorta is small and ascends vertically (Figs. 8.37 and 8.38).168 The trachea is not deviated by an aortic arch and is therefore midline.168 The x-ray shows increased pulmonary venous and pulmonary arterial vascularity with enlargement of the left ventricle (see Figs. 8.39 and 8.37).191,201 Isolated interruption of the aortic arch without a ductus or a ventricular septal defect is radiologically similar to coarctation of the aorta, including rib notching.169,172,202 Whether the notching is bilateral or unilateral depends on the site of interruption, the origin of the subclavian arteries, and the length of survival.168,169

paragraphs.text: The typical clinical picture of interruption of the aortic arch is an acyanotic neonate who initially appears well but who suddenly becomes ill when the ductus arteriosus constricts and deprives the trunk and lower limbs of arterial circulation while diverting pulmonary arterial blood into the lungs and into the left side of the heart. Tachypnea and symmetric cyanosis develop, the femoral pulses disappear, and the chest x-ray exhibits pulmonary venous
paragraphs.heading: Summary

paragraphs.text: congestion with progressive cardiac enlargement. When the interruption is proximal to the left subclavian artery, the left brachial arterial pulse disappears as well. There is either no murmur or an inconspicuous early systolic decrescendo murmur through the ventricular septal defect. The electrocardiogram shows peaked right atrial P waves and right ventricular hypertrophy, but if survival permits, biventricular hypertrophy emerges. Echocardiography identifies the interrupted arch. The ascending aorta takes a straight cephalad course and is small compared to the dilated pulmonary trunk. Continuity between pulmonary trunk, ductus, and descending aorta creates a smooth, unbroken contour. A leftward and posterior malaligned ventricular septal defect is the rule when the interruption is between the left carotid and left subclavian arteries. An aortopulmonary window is likely if the ventricular septum is intact.

figures.caption: Fig. 8.7 ​A 55-year-old man with near interruption of the descending thoracic aorta. (A) CT angiogram, sagittal view demonstrating severe coarctation resulting in near interruption of the proximal descending aorta (*) distal to the take-off of the left subclavian artery. Note the web of large arterial collaterals (arrows) bypassing the coarctation and entering the descending thoracic aorta below the level of obstruction. (B) CT angiogram, coronal view of the chest wall just beneath the sternum demonstrating enlarged mammary arteries (arrows) serving as off-loading collaterals from the subclavian arteries above the level of coarctation. (C) Simultaneous ascending aortic and femoral arterial pressure tracings demonstrating a 50 mm Hg peak to peak systolic gradient; the mean arterial pressure difference, however, is less than 15 mm Hg. This is due to the extensive web of arterial collaterals as seen in panels A and B supplying a sufficient amount of arterial flow to the arterial system below the level of coarctation in order to maintain basal perfusion and avoid resting ischemia. However, this patient reports near disabling claudication of the lower limbs with ambulation up one flight of stairs which confirms that the collateral circulation is sufficient at rest or with minimal activity but cannot supply sufficient arterial blood flow to avoid ischemia with more strenuous lower extremity exercises.

figures.caption: Fig. 8.32 ​Illustration of the anatomic and circulatory derangements in the three types of complete aortic interruption. The descending aorta (DAo) is continuous with the pulmonary artery (PA) via a nonrestrictive patent ductus arteriosus (*). A large ventricular septal defect provides the left ventricle with access to the descending aorta via pulmonary trunk/ductus/descending aortic continuity. The red coloration denotes highly oxygenated blood that is being ejected from the left ventricle via the ascending aorta (Asc Ao). The blue coloration denotes deoxygenated/mixed-blood return ejected into the PA by both the right and left ventricles and then shunting right to left via a large patent ductus arteriosus (*). (A) Type A—Interruption of the distal arch is distal to the left subclavian artery (LSCA). (B) Type B—Interruption is the commonest type. The Asc Ao gives rise to the innominate artery (Innom A.) and to the left carotid artery (LCA). The interruption is in the mid-aortic arch. The LSCA arises distal to the obstruction. (C) Type C—The interruption is within the proximal arch distal to the Innom A.

8 8 Coarctation of the Aorta and Interrupted Aortic Arch

### HISTORICAL NOTES

In 1760, the Prussian anatomist Johann Friedreich Meckel characterized coarctation of the aorta as an “extraordinary dilatation of the heart which came from the fact that the aortic conduit was too narrow.”1 Saul Jarcho’s historical papers underscored the accuracy of early accounts of this congenital malformation.1–5

### COARCTATION OF THE AORTA Anatomic Considerations

Coarctation of the aorta is typically located near the aortic attachment of the ligamentum arteriosum or patent ductus arteriosus (Figs. 8.1A and 8.2). An obtuse indentation in the posterolateral wall of the aorta corresponds to the location of an internal ridge or shelf that eccentrically narrows the aortic lumen, hence the term coarctatus (Latin, contracted or tightened). The ridge that forms the coarctation consists of smooth muscle, fibrous tissue, and elastic tissue similar in composition to a muscular arterial ductus (see Chapter 17).6 Intimal proliferation distal to the ridge narrows the lumen.6 The junction between the ductus and the elastic aorta is clearly defined, with the extension of ductal tissue into the aortic wall not exceeding 30% of the aortic circumference. In preductal coarctation, however, ductal tissue forms a circumferential sling that extends around the aorta.7 In juxtaductal coarctation, ductal tissue is not a significant part of the aortic wall.7 The coarctation ridge is thought to represent the original wall of the distal left sixth aortic arch (see Chapter 17). The neural crest is believed to play a role in the pathogenesis of some types of coarctation.7

The common form of aortic coarctation is represented by a localized constriction containing the ridge or shelf as just described.6 Less commonly, a relatively long segment of constriction extends beyond the left subclavian artery. Rarely, congenital coarctation is in the mid-thoracic aorta.8 Tubular hypoplasia refers to a uniform narrowing within the aortic arch.6 Localized coarctation and tubular hypoplasia sometimes coexist.

The mechanisms that account for the typical location of coarctation take into account a number of variables: (1) the quantitative morphology and growth of the aortic arch in the normal fetus,9–11 (2) the site of the aortic orifice of the ductus arteriosus, (3) the presence of ductal tissue in the coarctation, 6 (4) constriction of ductal tissue immediately after birth, and (5) coarctation in the presence of a widely patent ductus in the fetus12,13 and after birth.6 Current consensus favors an interplay between aortic growth and blood flow.9–11 High-resolution echocardiographic imaging in the normal fetus has disclosed progressive tapering of the diameter of the aortic arch at all gestational ages with the smallest diameter at the isthmus.9 Tapering is believed to reflect the relative proportion of fetal cardiac output traversing each aortic segment. The smallest proportion traverses the isthmus, which maintains its smaller dimension relative to the remainder of the aortic arch well into postnatal life, especially in premature infants.9 Neonatal coarctation is characterized by hypoplasia of the transverse aorta in the presence of a relatively large pulmonary trunk, a combination that is believed to reflect an in utero decrease in aortic arch flow together with an increase in flow through the main pulmonary artery and ductus.11

The coarctation ridge is located either immediately proximal to the aortic insertion of the ductus, or opposite the aortic insertion (juxtaductal), or immediately distal to the aortic insertion.6,14,15 Infants with a juxtaductal coarctation show no signs of aortic obstruction as long as the ductus is widely patent, assuring unobstructed pulmonary trunk/ductus/descending aortic continuity. When the ductus closes, the coarctation becomes apparent immediately and dramatically, and the femoral pulses disappear. The left subclavian artery is dilated because coarctation is usually located immediately distal to its origin (see Figs. 8.1A and 8.3A). However, coarctation may lie at or proximal to the left subclavian orifice, compromising its lumen (see Fig. 8.1B and see Fig. 8.27, later). Exceptionally, the right subclavian artery arises distal to the coarctation (see Fig. 8.1C) or the coarctation is in a right aortic arch.16

Coarctation of the abdominal aorta can be part of a non-congenital systemic vascular disorder such as Takayasu arteritis or von Recklinghausen’s disease, but it can also be congenital and is therefore appropriate for inclusion here.17–20 Abdominal coarctation is rare, accounting for 0.5% to 2% of all varieties of aortic coarctation,18 and can be suprarenal, infrarenal, or inter-renal.18 Systemic hypertension is believed to be due to the involvement of the renal artery.20 A congenital etiology is based on the combination of a localized hourglass deformity with an intraluminal membrane, occurrence at a young age, absence of a systemic vascular disorder, and slow progression with the development of extensive collaterals.20

Pseudocoarctation refers to a rare anomaly characterized by buckling or kinking of the aorta in the vicinity of the ligamentum arteriosum, resulting in elongation, tortuosity, and dilatation of the distal aortic arch and the proximal descending aorta (Fig. 8.3).21–25 Occasionally, pseudocoarctation involves the abdominal aorta.26 Pseudo signifies the absence of a gradient at the site of the localized external deformity, absence of collaterals, and absence of systemic hypertension, although refractory hypertension has been reported.27 Occasionally, there is a transformation from pseudocoarctation to true coarctation.28 The femoral pulses are sometimes reduced because of the damping effect of sharp angulation of the aortic arch (Fig. 8.4).22 Thin-walled saccular aneurysms may form in the distal segment,21 spontaneous rupture and dissection have been reported in the proximal descending thoracic aorta29 and in the ascending aorta,30 and bicuspid aortic valve may coexist.31 The strongest association is with a functionally normal, stenotic, or incompetent bicuspid aortic valve (Fig. 8.5B and see Chapter 7)32,33 characterized by a fusion of the right and left coronary cusps.33,34 When aortic dissection occurs with coarctation that co-exists with a bicuspid aortic valve, adverse outcomes are more pronounced, suggesting that the bicuspid aortic valve may represent an advanced manifestation of a more diffuse arteriopathy.35

Coarctation of the aorta is usually and simplistically regarded as isolated obstruction of the aortic isthmus,36 but in fact is a widespread disorder in which isthmic obstruction is only one of a cluster of abnormalities that include the proximal and distal paracoarctation aorta, the ascending and transverse aorta, the coronary arteries, conduit arteries (radial, brachial, carotid), the retinal vascular bed, dissecting aneurysm, cerebral aneurysms, vascular rings, and systemic hypertension. A decrease in left ventricular interpapillary muscle distance is common37 and culminates in the single papillary muscle of a parachute mitral valve

### Physiologic Consequences

The pathogenesis of systemic hypertension in coarctation of the aorta has been the subject of three theories. The mechanical theory focuses on resistance at the site of obstruction. This theory in itself cannot be sustained but is central to the neural theory that involves the sensitivity of carotid sinus baroreceptors and the distensibility characteristics of the precoarctation aorta.60 The proximal aortic segment of coarctation has an increase in collagen and a decrease in smooth muscle60 that are responsible for an increase in stiffness and a decrease in distensibility.61 The poorly compliant precoarctation aorta is responsible for the elevation of systolic blood pressure at rest, the disproportionate rise during isotonic exercise,62,63 and the resetting of carotid sinus baroreceptors to operate at higher pressures.60,62 The renal theory of pathogenesis takes into account a unique feature of coarctation hypertension, namely, that the elevated blood pressure is confined to the upper extremities. Accordingly, the renal arteries are exposed to the neurohumoral effects of hypertension but not the hydraulic effects. The coarctation gradient increases during isotonic exercise, which is accompanied by a disproportionate increase in systolic pressure,64 an exaggeration of the inherent disproportionate systolic hypertension related to the rigidity of the precoarctation aortic wall. The response of the mean blood pressure to exercise is approximately the same as in controls.65 Experimental hypertension has been produced by aortic constriction that assigns the renal arteries to the distal low-pressure zone.66 When the constriction is below the renal arteries, blood pressure remains normal.66,67 Toxemia of pregnancy is not a feature of coarctation hypertension.

### The History

The male/female ratio of coarctation is 1.4:1 to 3:1.70 Familial recurrence has occurred in siblings, in monozygotic twins, in parent and child,71–76 and as an autosomal dominant in four generations.77 True coarctation and pseudocoarctation have been reported in siblings.78 Turner syndrome (see Physical Appearance) cannot be transmitted because of sterility, but seven women in three generations of one family had Turner syndrome attributed to loss of the short arm of one X chromosome that permitted transmission from phenotypically normal female carriers with a balanced X-1 translocation.79 There is a peak seasonal incidence of coarctation from September through November and from January through March.80 The reported rarity of coarctation in African Americans is open to question.81,82

### The Arterial Pulse

Abnormal differences in upper and lower extremity arterial pulses and blood pressure are hallmarks of coarctation of the aorta. If proper attention were given to these pulses, few or no diagnoses would be missed.91,132 Two methods have been advocated for comparing upper and lower extremity arterial pulsations. One method compares femoral and radial pulses; the other method compares femoral and brachial pulses. Normally, radial and femoral pulses are sensed as synchronous so that any femoral delay is considered abnormal. Positioning the patient’s wrist next to the groin is believed to facilitate comparison. In infants and newborns, the brachial artery is more readily palpated than the tiny radial artery, which is surrounded by subcutaneous fat pads (Fig. 8.14B). Comparative palpation of brachial and femoral pulses can be achieved by placing a thumb on each (see Fig. 8.14A).132 The slight delay in perceived arrival time of the normal femoral pulse (15 ms in adults, less in infants and children) is easily sensed as a norm against which even slight deviations can be judged. When palpating the femoral pulse in an infant, the patient must be allowed to relax its legs voluntarily because forceful restraint can decrease or abolish a normal femoral pulse.

What is perceived as an abnormal delay of the femoral pulse in coarctation is not a delay in arrival time but instead a slow rate of rise to a delayed peak (Fig. 8.15). The presence of a normal femoral pulse effectively eliminates all but mild coarctation provided the aortic valve is functioning normally (see later). ### Precordial Movement and Palpation

The left ventricular impulse varies from normal to the sustained heaving impulse of pressure overload hypertrophy.132 In symptomatic infants with biventricular failure, the right ventricular impulse is dynamic because the pressure overload of pulmonary hypertension is coupled with volume overload of a right-to-left shunt through the foramen ovale. Suprasternal notch systolic thrills are frequent in uncomplicated coarctation, but precordial thrills are generated by coexisting bicuspid aortic stenosis.

### Auscultation

Coarctation of the aorta is associated with systolic, diastolic, and continuous murmurs (Fig. 8.17). An ejection sound is an auscultatory sign of a coexisting bicuspid aortic valve (see Figs. 8.17 and 8.18). Systolic murmurs originate from three sources (see Fig. 8.17): (1) arterial collaterals, (2) the coarctation itself, and (3) the brachiocephalic arteries. That murmurs can originate in collateral arteries is based on observations that localized superficial collateral murmurs are abolished by compression and that murmurs have been recorded from the surfaces of surgically exposed collateral arteries.145 A murmur cannot be generated across coarctation when the obstruction is complete (see Fig. 8.7B), but murmurs are prominent because arterial collaterals are well developed (see Fig. 8.7A and C).145 The widespread anatomic distribution of the collateral arterial circulation accounts for the widespread thoracic distribution of accompanying murmurs.146 Collateral murmurs are crescendo-decrescendo and are delayed in onset and termination because they originate at a distance from the heart (see Figs. 8.17, 8.19, and 8.20).145 Widely distributed thoracic murmurs constitute presumptive evidence of collateral circulation, but in young children, collaterals may be well developed without generating murmurs, and in occasional adults with abundant collaterals, murmurs are inconspicuous.

### Summary

Coarctation of the aorta will not be overlooked if attention is given to upper and lower extremity arterial pulses and blood pressure during routine physical examination. The diagnosis is evident when systemic hypertension is accompanied by reduced femoral pulses. Aortic coarctation is a widespread disorder in which isthmic obstruction is only one of an array of abnormalities that include abnormalities of the proximal and distal paracoarctation aorta, abnormalities of the ascending and transverse aorta, the conduit arteries (radial, brachial, carotid), the retinal vascular bed, in addition to systemic hypertension, dissecting aneurysm, cerebral aneurysms, and vascular rings. Minor symptoms include headache, epistaxis, and leg fatigue. Major complications are congestive heart failure, especially in infants, rupture or dissection of the paracoarctation aorta, infective endarteritis, and rupture of an aneurysm of the circle of Willis. The physical appearance of XO Turner syndrome increases the probability of coarctation. Pulse pressure proximal to the coarctation increases with age, resulting in conspicuous carotid and suprasternal notch pulsations. Collateral arterial pulsations should be sought beneath the skin, especially around the scapulae. Tortuous U-shaped retinal arterioles are distinctive. A left ventricular impulse occupies the apex. A right ventricular impulse is reserved for symptomatic infants with heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, and a right-to-left shunt across a patent foramen ovale. Auscultatory

signs include widespread thoracic systolic murmurs through arterial collaterals and a posterior systolic or continuous murmur over the coarctation site. Systolic murmurs are especially prominent in the suprasternal notch and along the left sternal border over internal mammary collaterals. Auscultatory signs in infants are limited to the posterior interscapular murmur over the coarctation. Electrocardiographic criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy reflect increased afterload. Right ventricular hypertrophy characterizes the electrocardiogram of symptomatic infants. Notching of the third to eighth posterior ribs is a radiologic feature of major diagnostic importance but is seldom present before age six years. Dilatation of both the left subclavian artery and the proximal descending aorta are useful radiologic signs in children too young to have rib notching. Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiograms with Doppler interrogation and color flow imaging identify the coarctation and determine its severity.

### INTERRUPTION OF THE AORTIC ARCH

The thoracic aorta lends itself to the segmental analysis of its ascending portion, arch, isthmus, and descending portion. Atresia or interruption of the aortic arch is the ultimate expression of obstructive thoracic aortic anomalies that begin with isthmic coarctation. The embryogenesis of these anomalies is similar, if not identical.

Interruption of the aortic arch was first described in the 18th century by Raphael Steidele of the University of Vienna.159 Steidele’s complex is occasionally applied as an eponym to this rare malformation,160,161 which is characterized by a complete anatomic discontinuity or by an atretic fibrous strand between the aortic arch and the descending aorta (Fig. 8.32).162–165 The classification of complete interruption by Celoria and Patton163 refers to one of three sites,160,161,165,166 two of which were described in 1927 by Maude Abbott.167 Interruption between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries (type B) (see Figs. 8.32 and 8.33) is more common than interruption distal to the left subclavian artery (type A). The least common site is between the innominate artery and the left carotid artery (type C) (Fig. 8.34).163,168,169 Subtypes are based on the anomalous origin of the right subclavian artery.134,168,170 Rarely, interruption is in a right aortic arch.171

Interruption of the aortic arch seldom occurs as an isolated anomaly.172–175 Patent ductus arteriosus and ventricular septal defect are coexisting malformations upon which tenuous neonatal survival depends. The clinical picture in infants is largely determined by the patency of the ductus arteriosus, which provides nonrestrictive flow from the pulmonary trunk into the descending aorta (see Fig. 8.32).160,164,165 In the majority of patients with interrupted aortic arch, the ductus is histologically mature with prominent intimal cushions that prefigure constriction. In a minority of patients, an immature ductus is devoid of intimal cushions and has marked elastification that sets the stage for persistent patency. A ventricular septal defect almost invariably coexists when the interruption is between the left carotid and left subclavian arteries (type B), and it coexists in about 50% of interruptions distal to the left subclavian artery (type A).43,160,164–166,168,173 A posterior malaligned ventricular septal defect is the rule when the interrupted arch is between the left carotid and left subclavian arteries (type B).162,166,176 Defects in the perimembranous and muscular septum are uncommon.43 Posterior deviation of the infundibular septum encroaches on the left ventricular outflow tract and causes subaortic obstruction.43,166 When the ventricular septum is intact, a physiologically equivalent aortopulmonary window is almost always present,177 and the interrupted arch is distal to the left subclavian artery (type A).177

### Precordial Movement and Palpation

An isolated right ventricular impulse is palpated in infants with interruption of the aortic arch because of obligatory pulmonary hypertension and is associated with a nonrestrictive patent ductus arteriosus and ventricular septal defect. A left ventricular impulse is absent despite the left-to-right shunt at the ventricular level because blood entering the pulmonary trunk is diverted through the ductus into the descending aorta rather than through the pulmonary circulation into the left side of the heart (see Fig. 8.32). Interruption of the aortic arch without patent ductus or ventricular septal defect results in a left ventricular impulse analogous to coarctation of the aorta.181

### Auscultation

Murmurs are negligible or absent.165 The ductus is silent because the shunt is entirely right-to-left through a single nonrestrictive arterial conduit formed by continuity of the pulmonary trunk, ductus, and descending aorta. Murmurs originating through the ventricular septal defect are early systolic, decrescendo, and grade 3/6 or less.191,201 A continuous murmur has been attributed to collateral circulation connecting the ascending and descending aortas.191 Diastolic murmurs due to pulmonary hypertensive pulmonary regurgitation165 are introduced by a loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound. Interruption of the aortic arch without a ductus or ventricular septal defect presents with auscultatory signs similar to those of imperforate coarctation, with widespread collateral murmurs that include the head, especially behind the ears.172,181,202

### The Electrocardiogram

Peaked right atrial P waves and right ventricular hypertrophy are electrocardiographic features in the neonate with interruption of the aortic arch, ventricular septal defect, and patent ductus arteriosus (Fig. 8.35).201 Biventricular hypertrophy is in response to left ventricular volume overload and persistent right ventricular pressure overload (Fig. 8.36).165 Interruption without patent ductus or ventricular septal defect results in right ventricular hypertrophy in infants,134 but left ventricular hypertrophy in older patients.

### The X-Ray

The cardiac silhouette enlarges, and pulmonary venous congestion develops rapidly when the closure of the ductus arteriosus suddenly causes an increase in pulmonary blood flow and volume overload of the left ventricle. The aortic knuckle is absent because the ascending aorta is small and ascends vertically (Figs. 8.37 and 8.38).168 The trachea is not deviated by an aortic arch and is therefore midline.168 The x-ray shows increased pulmonary venous and pulmonary arterial vascularity with enlargement of the left ventricle (see Figs. 8.39 and 8.37).191,201 Isolated interruption of the aortic arch without a ductus or a ventricular septal defect is radiologically similar to coarctation of the aorta, including rib notching.169,172,202 Whether the notching is bilateral or unilateral depends on the site of interruption, the origin of the subclavian arteries, and the length of survival.168,169

### Summary

The typical clinical picture of interruption of the aortic arch is an acyanotic neonate who initially appears well but who suddenly becomes ill when the ductus arteriosus constricts and deprives the trunk and lower limbs of arterial circulation while diverting pulmonary arterial blood into the lungs and into the left side of the heart. Tachypnea and symmetric cyanosis develop, the femoral pulses disappear, and the chest x-ray exhibits pulmonary venous

congestion with progressive cardiac enlargement. When the interruption is proximal to the left subclavian artery, the left brachial arterial pulse disappears as well. There is either no murmur or an inconspicuous early systolic decrescendo murmur through the ventricular septal defect. The electrocardiogram shows peaked right atrial P waves and right ventricular hypertrophy, but if survival permits, biventricular hypertrophy emerges. Echocardiography identifies the interrupted arch. The ascending aorta takes a straight cephalad course and is small compared to the dilated pulmonary trunk. Continuity between pulmonary trunk, ductus, and descending aorta creates a smooth, unbroken contour. A leftward and posterior malaligned ventricular septal defect is the rule when the interruption is between the left carotid and left subclavian arteries. An aortopulmonary window is likely if the ventricular septum is intact.

Fig. 8.7 ​A 55-year-old man with near interruption of the descending thoracic aorta.
